intro: Tranekær is a village in the north of Langeland, the long island south of Funen, gathered around a red castle whose grounds outside the moats are open to walkers. At the edge of the castle woods, above an open meadow, a reader found an old oak with a tangle of silver-white dead limbs and sent us its photograph. We do not yet know its age or girth.
meta_description: An old oak with silver-white dead limbs at the edge of the castle woods in Tranekær on Langeland, sent by a reader: where it stands and what we know.
question_meta: The remarkable tree at Tranekær on Langeland: an old oak with silver-white dead limbs at the edge of the castle woods, sent by a reader.
question_answer: The Silver-Limbed Oak of Tranekær stands at the edge of the castle woods, about half a kilometre east of Tranekær Slot on Langeland. The castle grounds outside the moats are open to walkers.
question_context: A reader walking at Tranekær in November 2026 sent us a photograph of this oak from the meadow at the edge of the castle woods. It stands out even among the old oaks around it. A thick, dark trunk leans out of the undergrowth and forks into two stems that carry a high crown, and from its lower half a tangle of dead limbs, bleached silver-white, twists out sideways, bright against the darker wood. Dead wood like this is normal on an old oak, which can keep it for decades, and it is valuable habitat for beetles, fungi and woodpeckers. Tranekær Slot, the red castle the village grew around, is not open inside except on guided tours, but its grounds outside the moats are open to walkers all year, with paths through the park. The oak is about half a kilometre east of the castle. We have no age, girth or exact species for it yet, and we would like readers who know it to tell us.

faq.q: What is the remarkable tree at Tranekær?
faq.a: An old oak at the edge of the castle woods, with a tangle of silver-white dead limbs, sent to us by a reader.
The castle grounds outside the moats are open to walkers all year. The castle itself opens only for guided tours.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: Late autumn and winter, when the leaves are down and the pale dead limbs stand out against the wood.

trees.story:
A reader walking the woods of Tranekær on Langeland in November stopped at the edge of a meadow and sent us this oak.

Even among the old oaks around it, this one stands apart. Its trunk leans out of the undergrowth, thick, dark and furrowed, and then forks into two great stems that climb into a high crown of crooked branches. Lower down it carries a tangle of dead limbs, bleached silver-white and twisting out sideways like antlers, so that from across the grass the tree seems to glow against the darker wood behind it. Old oaks keep dead wood like this for decades, and for beetles, fungi and woodpeckers those pale limbs are some of the richest wood in the forest.

Tranekær is the village around the red castle of the same name in the north of Langeland, and the castle's grounds outside the moats are open to walkers. The oak stands about half a kilometre east of the castle, where the wood meets an open meadow.

We do not know its age, its girth or exactly which oak it is. If you have stood under it, tell us what you measured or what you know of it, and we will add it with your figures.

Come in late autumn, when the leaves are down and the silver limbs show best.
